You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# ast-grep(sg) ast-grep(sg) is a CLI tool for code structural search, lint, and rewriting. ## What is ast-grep? ast-grep is an [abstract syntax tree](https://dev.to/balapriya/abstract-syntax-tree-ast-explained-in-plain-english-1h38) based tool to search code by pattern code. Think of it as your old-friend [`grep`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grep), but matching AST nodes instead of text. You can write patterns as if you are writing ordinary code. It will match all code that has the same syntactical structure. You can use `$` sign + upper case letters as a [wildcard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildcard_character), e.g. `$MATCH`, to match any single AST node. Think of it as [regular expression dot](https://regexone.com/lesson/wildcards_dot) `.`, except it is not textual. Try the [online playground](https://ast-grep.github.io/playground.html) for a taste! ## Screenshot ![demo](https://ast-grep.github.io/image/search-replace.png) See more screenshots on the [website](https://ast-grep.github.io/). ## Installation You can install ast-grep from npm, pip, cargo, cargo-binstall, homebrew, scoop, mise, or MacPorts: ```bash npm install --global @ast-grep/cli # `pnpm approve-builds` may be needed pip install ast-grep-cli brew install ast-grep cargo install ast-grep --locked cargo binstall ast-grep # install via scoop scoop install main/ast-grep # install via MacPorts sudo port install ast-grep # try ast-grep in nix-shell nix-shell -p ast-grep # try ast-grep with mise mise use -g ast-grep ``` [Packages](https://repology.org/project/ast-grep/versions) are available on other platforms too. ## Command line usage ast-grep has the following form: ```bash ast-grep --pattern 'var code = $PATTERN' --rewrite 'let code = new $PATTERN' --lang ts ``` ### Examples * Rewrite code using null coalescing operator: ```bash ast-grep -p '$A && $A()' -l ts -r '$A?.()' ``` * Rewrite Zodios code: ```bash ast-grep -p 'new Zodios($URL, $CONF as const,)' -l ts -r 'new Zodios($URL, $CONF)' -i ``` ## Features ast-grep helps you search and replace code based on abstract syntax trees. It can help you do lightweight static analysis and massive scale code manipulation in an intuitive way. Key features: * **Intuitive pattern syntax**: Write patterns that look like ordinary code you would write every day (the pattern is isomorphic to code). * **jQuery-like API**: For AST traversal and manipulation. * **YAML configuration**: Write new linting rules or code modifications using YAML. * **Fast and scalable**: Utilizes multiple cores for performance. * **Beautiful CLI**: User-friendly command line interface. ## Use Cases * **Open-source library authors**: Help your library users adopt breaking changes more easily. * **Tech leads**: Enforce code best practices tailored to your business needs. * **Security researchers**: Write security rules much faster. ## More Information Visit the [official website](https://ast-grep.github.io/) for complete documentation and tutorials. ## Schemas JSON schemas for ast-grep rule configuration are available in the `schemas/` directory. pub fn run_args(cmd: Command) -> Command {
    let cmd = cmd
        .arg(
            Arg::new("pattern")
                .short('p')
                .long("pattern")
                .value_name("PATTERN")
                .required(true)
                .help("AST pattern to match"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("selector")
                .long("selector")
                .value_name("KIND")
                .help("AST kind to extract sub-part of pattern to match")
                .long_help("AST kind to extract sub-part of pattern to match.\n\nselector defines the sub-syntax node kind that is the actual matcher of the pattern. See https://ast-grep.github.io/guide/rule-config/atomic-rule.html#pattern-object."),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("rewrite")
                .short('r')
                .long("rewrite")
                .value_name("FIX")
                .help("String to replace the matched AST node"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("lang")
                .short('l')
                .long("lang")
                .value_name("LANG")
                .value_parser(crate::lang::LangParser)
                .help(format!("The language of the pattern. Supported languages are:\n{}", LANG_LIST))
                .long_help("The language of the pattern. For full language list, visit https://ast-grep.github.io/reference/languages.html"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("debug_query")
                .long("debug-query")
                .value_name("format")
                .num_args(0..=1)
                .require_equals(true)
                .default_missing_value("pattern")
                .requires("lang")
                .value_parser(PossibleValuesParser::new([
                    pv("pattern", "Print the query parsed in Pattern format"),
                    pv("ast", "Print the query in tree-sitter AST format, only named nodes are shown"),
                    pv("cst", "Print the query in tree-sitter CST format, both named and unnamed nodes are shown"),
                    pv("sexp", "Print the query in S-expression format"),
                ]))
                .help("Print query pattern's tree-sitter AST. Requires lang be set explicitly"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("strictness")
                .long("strictness")
                .value_name("STRICTNESS")
                .value_parser(PossibleValuesParser::new([
                    pv("cst", "Match exact all node"),
                    pv("smart", "Match all node except source trivial nodes"),
                    pv("ast", "Match only ast nodes"),
                    pv("relaxed", "Match ast node except comments"),
                    pv("signature", "Match ast node except comments, without text"),
                    pv("template", "Similar to smart but match text only, node kinds are ignored"),
                ]))
                .help("The strictness of the pattern"),
        )
        .arg(config_arg());
    let cmd = input_args(cmd);
    let cmd = output_args(cmd);
    let cmd = context_args(cmd);
    cmd.arg(
        Arg::new("paths")
            .value_name("PATHS")
            .action(ArgAction::Append)
            .default_value(".")
            .help("The paths to search. You can provide multiple paths separated by spaces"),
    )
}

                .long("selector")
                .value_name("KIND")
                .help("AST kind to extract sub-part of pattern to match")
                .long_help("AST kind to extract sub-part of pattern to match.\n\nselector defines the sub-syntax node kind that is the actual matcher of the pattern. See https://ast-grep.github.io/guide/rule-config/atomic-rule.html#pattern-object."),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("rewrite")
                .short('r')
                .long("rewrite")
                .value_name("FIX")
                .help("String to replace the matched AST node"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("lang")
                .short('l')
                .long("lang")
                .value_name("LANG")
                .value_parser(crate::lang::LangParser)
                .help(format!("The language of the pattern. Supported languages are:\n{}", LANG_LIST))
                .long_help("The language of the pattern. For full language list, visit https://ast-grep.github.io/reference/languages.html"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("debug_query")
                .long("debug-query")
                .value_name("format")
                .num_args(0..=1)
                .require_equals(true)
                .default_missing_value("pattern")
                .requires("lang")
                .value_parser(PossibleValuesParser::new([
                    pv("pattern", "Print the query parsed in Pattern format"),
                    pv("ast", "Print the query in tree-sitter AST format, only named nodes are shown"),
                    pv("cst", "Print the query in tree-sitter CST format, both named and unnamed nodes are shown"),
                    pv("sexp", "Print the query in S-expression format"),
                ]))
                .help("Print query pattern's tree-sitter AST. Requires lang be set explicitly"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("strictness")
                .long("strictness")
                .value_name("STRICTNESS")
                .value_parser(PossibleValuesParser::new([
                    pv("cst", "Match exact all node"),
                    pv("smart", "Match all node except source trivial nodes"),
                    pv("ast", "Match only ast nodes"),
                    pv("relaxed", "Match ast node except comments"),
                    pv("signature", "Match ast node except comments, without text"),
                    pv("template", "Similar to smart but match text only, node kinds are ignored"),
                ]))
                .help("The strictness of the pattern"),
        )
        .arg(config_arg());
    let cmd = input_args(cmd);
    let cmd = output_args(cmd);
    let cmd = context_args(cmd);
    cmd.arg(
        Arg::new("paths")
            .value_name("PATHS")
            .action(ArgAction::Append)
            .default_value(".")
            .help("The paths to search. You can provide multiple paths separated by spaces"),
    )
}

fn severity_arg(name: &'static str, help: &'static str, long: &'static str) -> Arg {
    Arg::new(name)
        .long(name)
        .value_name("RULE_ID")
        .num_args(0..)
        .require_equals(true)
        .value_delimiter(',')
        .action(ArgAction::Append)
        .help(help)
        .long_help(long)
}

pub fn scan_cmd() -> Command {
    let cmd = Command::new("scan")
        .about("Scan and rewrite code by configuration")
        .arg(
            Arg::new("rule")
                .short('r')
                .long("rule")
                .value_name("RULE_FILE")
                .help("Scan the codebase with the single rule located at the path RULE_FILE")
                .long_help("Scan the codebase with the single rule located at the path RULE_FILE.\n\nIt is useful to run single rule without project setup or sgconfig.yml."),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("inline_rules")
                .long("inline-rules")
                .value_name("RULE_TEXT")
                .conflicts_with("rule")
                .help("Scan the codebase with a rule defined by the provided RULE_TEXT")
                .long_help("Scan the codebase with a rule defined by the provided RULE_TEXT.\n\nUse this argument if you want to test a rule without creating a YAML file on disk. You can run multiple rules by separating them with `---` in the RULE_TEXT. --inline-rules is incompatible with --rule."),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("format")
                .long("format")
                .value_name("FORMAT")
                .value_parser(["github", "sarif"])
                .conflicts_with("json")
                .help("Output warning/error messages in different formats")
                .long_help("Output warning/error messages in different formats.\n\nSupported formats: GitHub Action, SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format)."),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("report_style")
                .long("report-style")
                .value_name("REPORT_STYLE")
                .default_value("rich")
                .value_parser(PossibleValuesParser::new([
                    pv("rich", "Output a richly formatted diagnostic, with source code previews"),
                    pv("medium", "Output a condensed diagnostic, with a line number, severity, message and notes (if any)"),
                    pv("short", "Output a short diagnostic, with a line number, severity, and message"),
                ])),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("include_metadata")
                .long("include-metadata")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Include rule metadata in the json output")
                .long_help("Include rule metadata in the json output.\n\nThis flags requires --json output. Default is false."),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("filter")
                .long("filter")
                .value_name("REGEX")
                .conflicts_with("rule")
                .help("Scan the codebase with rules with ids matching REGEX")
                .long_help("Scan the codebase with rules with ids matching REGEX.\n\nThis flags conflicts with --rule. It is useful to scan with a subset of rules from a large set of rule definitions within a project."),
        )
        .arg(config_arg())
        .arg(severity_arg("error", "Set rule severity to error", "Set rule severity to error\n\nThis flag sets the specified RULE_ID's severity to error. You can specify multiple rules by using the flag multiple times, e.g., `--error=RULE_1 --error=RULE_2`. If no RULE_ID is provided, all rules will be set to error, e.g., `--error`. Note, this flag must use `=` to specify its value."))
        .arg(severity_arg("warning", "Set rule severity to warning", "Set rule severity to warning\n\nThis flag sets the specified RULE_ID's severity to warning. You can specify multiple rules by using the flag multiple times. If no RULE_ID is provided, all rules will be set to warning. Note, this flag must use `=` to specify its value."))
        .arg(severity_arg("info", "Set rule severity to info", "Set rule severity to info\n\nThis flag sets the specified RULE_ID's severity to info. You can specify multiple rules by using the flag multiple times. If no RULE_ID is provided, all rules will be set to info. Note, this flag must use `=` to specify its value."))
        .arg(severity_arg("hint", "Set rule severity to hint", "Set rule severity to hint\n\nThis flag sets the specified RULE_ID's severity to hint. You can specify multiple rules by using the flag multiple times. If no RULE_ID is provided, all rules will be set to hint. Note, this flag must use `=` to specify its value."))
        .arg(severity_arg("off", "Turn off rule", "Turn off rule\n\nThis flag turns off the specified RULE_ID. You can disable multiple rules by using the flag multiple times. If no RULE_ID is provided, all rules will be turned off. Note, this flag must use `=` to specify its value."));
    let cmd = input_args(cmd);
    let cmd = output_args(cmd);
    let cmd = context_args(cmd);
    cmd.arg(
        Arg::new("max_results")
            .long("max-results")
            .value_name("NUM")
            .value_parser(clap::value_parser!(usize))
            .help("Show at most NUM results and stop running once the limit is reached")
            .long_help("Show at most NUM results and stop running once the limit is reached.\n\nUseful for big codebase to fail scan/search fast."),
    )
    .arg(
        Arg::new("paths")
            .value_name("PATHS")
            .action(ArgAction::Append)
            .default_value(".")
            .help("The paths to search. You can provide multiple paths separated by spaces"),
    )
}

pub fn test_cmd() -> Command {
    Command::new("test")
        .about("Test ast-grep rules")
        .arg(
            Arg::new("test_dir")
                .short('t')
                .long("test-dir")
                .value_name("TEST_DIR")
                .help("the directories to search test YAML files"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("snapshot_dir")
                .long("snapshot-dir")
                .value_name("SNAPSHOT_DIR")
                .help("Specify the directory name storing snapshots. Default to __snapshots__"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("skip_snapshot_tests")
                .long("skip-snapshot-tests")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .conflicts_with("update_all")
                .help("Only check if the test code is valid, without checking rule output. Turn it on when you want to ignore the output of rules. Conflicts with --update-all"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("update_all")
                .short('U')
                .long("update-all")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Update the content of all snapshots that have changed in test. Conflicts with --skip-snapshot-tests"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("interactive")
                .short('i')
                .long("interactive")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Start an interactive review to update snapshots selectively"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("filter")
                .short('f')
                .long("filter")
                .value_name("REGEX")
                .help("Only run rule test cases that matches REGEX"),
        )
        .arg(config_arg())
        .arg(
            Arg::new("include_off")
                .long("include-off")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Include `severity:off` rules in test")
                .long_help("Include `severity:off` rules in test\n\nast-grep will not run rules with `severity: off` by default. This option will include those rules in the test."),
        )
        .arg(color_arg())
}

pub fn new_cmd() -> Command {
    Command::new("new")
        .about("Create new ast-grep project or items like rules/tests")
        .subcommand(Command::new("project").about("Create an new project by scaffolding"))
        .subcommand(Command::new("rule").about("Create a new rule"))
        .subcommand(Command::new("test").about("Create a new test case"))
        .subcommand(Command::new("util").about("Create a new global utility rule"))
        .arg(Arg::new("name").value_name("NAME").help("The id of the item to create"))
        .arg(
            Arg::new("lang")
                .short('l')
                .long("lang")
                .value_name("LANG")
                .value_parser(crate::lang::LangParser)
                .help("The language of the item to create")
                .long_help("The language of the item to create.\n\nThis option is only available when creating rule and util."),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("yes")
                .short('y')
                .long("yes")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Accept all default options without interactive input during creation")
                .long_help("Accept all default options without interactive input during creation.\n\nYou need to provide all required arguments via command line if this flag is true. Please see the command description for the what arguments are required."),
        )
        .arg(config_arg())
}

pub fn lsp_cmd() -> Command {
    Command::new("lsp").about("Start language server").arg(config_arg())
}

pub fn completions_cmd() -> Command {
    Command::new("completions")
        .about("Generate shell completion script")
        .arg(
            Arg::new("shell")
                .value_name("SHELL")
                .value_parser(clap::value_parser!(clap_complete::Shell))
                .help("Output the completion file for given shell. If not provided, shell flavor will be inferred from environment"),
        )
        .arg(config_arg())
}

pub fn build_cli() -> Command {
    let cmd = Command::new("ast-grep")
        .version("0.42.1")
        .about("Search and Rewrite code at large scale using precise AST pattern")
        .long_about(LONG_ABOUT)
        .subcommand_required(true)
        .arg_required_else_help(true)
        .subcommand(
            run_args(Command::new("run"))
                .about("Run one time search or rewrite in command line. (default command)"),
        )
        .subcommand(scan_cmd())
        .subcommand(test_cmd())
        .subcommand(new_cmd())
        .subcommand(lsp_cmd())
        .subcommand(completions_cmd());
    cmd.arg(config_arg())
}

/// The command used when no subcommand is given (defaults to `run`).
pub fn build_default_run_cli() -> Command {
    let cmd = Command::new("ast-grep")
        .version("0.42.1")
        .about("Search and Rewrite code at large scale using precise AST pattern")
        .long_about(LONG_ABOUT);
    run_args(cmd)
}

content.text:
The work is complete and committed. Summary of what I built:

**Approach**: A from-scratch Rust reimplementation of the `ast-grep` CLI (v0.42.1), derived purely from observing the provided binary's behavior and the bundled docs/schemas. No tree-sitter was available offline, so I wrote my own parsers.

**Components** (all in `src/`):
- `cli.rs` – clap-builder CLI reproducing all help texts, usage lines, error messages, shell completions (bash/zsh/fish/elvish/powershell byte-identical), and the "default `run` command" dispatch quirk (`-p` without a subcommand).
- `parsers/js.rs` – hand-written JavaScript/TypeScript/TSX parser producing tree-sitter-compatible CSTs (node kinds, field names, byte ranges, error recovery approximation); verified identical to the original's `--debug-query=cst` on many samples.
- `parsers/python.rs` – Python parser (indentation blocks, f-strings, comprehensions, match, etc.) with tree-sitter-python node kinds.
- `parsers/json.rs`, `parsers/generic.rs` – JSON parser and a heuristic bracket/call/member fallback for the other 23 languages with per-language kind names.
- `pattern.rs`/`matcher.rs`/`meta_var.rs` – pattern compilation, `$A`/`$$A`/`$$$A`/`$_` meta-variables, and the matching algorithm (smart/cst/ast/relaxed/signature/template strictness, ellipsis semantics, trailing-trivia handling) reverse-engineered through extensive probing.
- `rule.rs`/`config.rs`/`transform.rs`/`fix.rs` – YAML rule configs (pattern/kind/regex/nthChild/range/inside/has/precedes/follows/all/any/not/matches, constraints, utils, transforms, rewriters, fix with expandStart/End, indentation-sensitive replacement), sgconfig projects, error messages with exit codes.
- `print/` + `diff.rs` – terminal printer (plain/heading/context/colors), unified diff with `similar`-compatible Myers alignment and word-level inline emphasis, codespan-style rich/medium/short diagnostics, JSON (pretty/stream/compact), GitHub and SARIF formats.
- `run.rs`, `scan.rs`, `test_cmd.rs`, `new_cmd.rs` – the subcommands including `--update-all`, snapshots, scaffolding, inspection tracing.

`compile.sh` builds offline with cargo (release) and produces `./executable`; build artifacts and the original binary are gitignored.
